questions.title: The anatomical plane dividing the body into equal right and left halves
questions.question: Which one of the following is the anatomical plane that divides the body into equal right and left halves?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A coronal (frontal) plane is a vertical plane running side to side, dividing the body into anterior and posterior parts, not right and left halves.
explanations.B: Correct. The median (midsagittal) plane is the single vertical anteroposterior plane that runs through the exact midline of the body, dividing it into equal right and left halves. It is the reference plane from which lateral and medial are measured, and every other sagittal plane (parasagittal) is defined only by its offset from this one central plane. Because it passes through the body's true centre, it is the only sagittal-type plane that produces two mirror-image halves rather than two unequal portions.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A transverse (horizontal) plane divides the body into upper (superior) and lower (inferior) parts, at whatever level it is taken, not into right and left halves.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A parasagittal plane is any plane parallel to the median plane but offset from the true midline; by definition it produces two unequal portions, not equal right and left halves.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "Frontal" is simply another name for the coronal plane, so it shares the same problem as option A: it divides the body into anterior and posterior parts, not right and left halves.

questions.learning_objective: State that the median plane divides the body into equal right and left halves.

questions.title: Relationship of the radius to the ulna
questions.question: Which term of the following describes the relationship of the radius to the ulna?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Proximal describes position along a limb's long axis (closer to the trunk), not the side-to-side relationship between the two forearm bones.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Distal, like proximal, describes position along the limb's long axis (further from the trunk), not a side-to-side relationship.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Medial would describe the ulna's position relative to the radius, not the radius's position relative to the ulna -- the two terms are opposites and are not interchangeable.
explanations.D: Correct. In the standard anatomical position, with the body erect and the palms facing forward, the radius is the lateral bone of the forearm and the ulna is the medial bone. This relationship is fixed by convention to the anatomical position and does not change with pronation or supination, even though the radius physically crosses over the ulna during those movements. "Lateral" and "medial" describe this side-to-side relationship specifically, distinguishing it from the length-axis terms proximal/distal and the front-to-back terms anterior/posterior.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Anterior describes a front-to-back relationship, which does not apply to two bones lying side by side in the same coronal plane of the forearm.

questions.learning_objective: State that the radius lies lateral to the ulna in the anatomical position.

questions.title: Moving the sole of the foot away from the median plane
questions.question: Moving the sole of the foot away from the median plane is called which one of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Extension is a straightening movement at a joint (increasing the joint angle), not a description of which way the sole of the foot faces.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Abduction is movement of a whole limb away from the body's midline; it is a distinct named movement from the specific foot movement of eversion, even though both involve moving "away" from a reference line.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Adduction is movement of a limb toward the midline, the opposite of abduction, and is not the term used for the sole-of-foot movement described here.
explanations.D: Correct. Eversion turns the sole of the foot to face laterally, away from the median plane, and occurs mainly at the subtalar and transverse tarsal joints, produced chiefly by peroneus (fibularis) longus and brevis. It is the direct opposite of inversion. Ankle sprains occur far more often in forced inversion than in forced eversion, because the lateral ankle ligaments are weaker than the strong deltoid (medial) ligament that resists eversion.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Inversion is the opposite movement, turning the sole to face medially (toward the median plane), produced chiefly by tibialis anterior and posterior -- the reverse of what the question describes.

questions.learning_objective: Identify eversion as the movement that turns the sole of the foot away from the median plane.

questions.title: The body region with no deep fascia
questions.question: Which of the following regions doesn't contain deep fascia?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The thigh has a well-developed deep fascia (the fascia lata), which invests the thigh muscles as a tight fibrous stocking.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The sole of the foot has a thickened deep fascia, the plantar aponeurosis, which supports the longitudinal arch of the foot.
explanations.C: Correct. The face is the classic exception among named body regions: it has only superficial fascia, with the muscles of facial expression lying directly within it and no deep fascial layer separating them from the skin. This absence is exactly why facial muscles, unlike limb muscles, can insert directly into the skin and produce fine movements of expression, rather than acting only on bone or joints through a fascial sheath. It is also why facial infections and swelling spread relatively superficially rather than being contained by a deep fascial compartment.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The arm has a deep fascia (the brachial fascia) investing its muscle compartments, continuous with the fascia of the forearm and shoulder.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The ankle region has deep fascia, thickened locally into the flexor, extensor and peroneal retinacula that hold the crossing tendons in place.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the face as the body region with no deep fascia.

questions.title: Muscle attachment as a thin sheet of fibrous tissue
questions.question: When the attachment of a muscle is in the form of a thin sheet of fibrous tissue, it is called which one of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A tendon is a cord-like fibrous attachment, concentrated into a rope-like band rather than spread out as a thin sheet.
explanations.B: Correct. An aponeurosis is a thin, broad, flattened sheet of dense fibrous tissue that attaches a muscle to bone or to other fascia, typically where a wide muscle (such as the external oblique or the epicranial muscles) needs a wide area of attachment rather than a single concentrated point. It differs from a tendon only in shape, not in tissue type -- both are dense regular fibrous connective tissue -- and the distinction is purely about whether the attachment is sheet-like or cord-like.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A retinaculum is a fibrous band that retains and holds tendons in place as they cross a joint (such as the flexor retinaculum at the wrist); it is not itself a muscle's primary attachment.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A raphe is a fibrous seam formed where the fasciae of two muscles meet and interdigitate in the midline (such as the pharyngeal or perineal raphe), not a broad sheet-like attachment of a single muscle.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "Fleshy" describes a muscle attaching directly by its muscle fibres without any intervening fibrous tissue at all, which is the opposite of the fibrous-sheet attachment the question describes.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the aponeurosis as the thin, sheet-like form of fibrous muscle attachment.

questions.title: Which bone is a short (miniature) long bone
questions.question: Which of the following is considered a short long bone?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The carpal bones are classed as short bones (a compact shell around cancellous bone, roughly cuboidal in shape), not as any type of long bone -- they have no shaft (diaphysis) at all.
explanations.B: Correct. A miniature (short) long bone -- the metacarpals, metatarsals and phalanges -- has a diaphysis like a typical long bone, but only one epiphysis, at one end, with the other end fusing to the shaft without its own separate ossification centre. This single-epiphysis pattern is exactly what separates a miniature long bone from a typical long bone (which has an epiphysis at each end) while still keeping it in the long-bone family rather than the short-bone family.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The clavicle is classed as a modified (atypical) long bone for different reasons entirely -- it has no medullary cavity and ossifies partly intramembranously -- not because it is a miniature long bone with one epiphysis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The radius is a typical long bone, with a diaphysis and a separately-ossifying epiphysis at each end (proximal and distal), which is the opposite of the single-epiphysis miniature pattern.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The ulna, like the radius, is a typical long bone with an epiphysis at each end, not a miniature long bone.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the phalanges as an example of a miniature (short) long bone.

questions.title: Structure responsible for growth of a long bone in thickness
questions.question: The structure responsible for the growth of a long bone in thickness is which one of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The epiphysis is the bone end itself, the site where the epiphyseal plate is located; it is not the tissue layer responsible for adding new bone width.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The epiphyseal (growth) plate is responsible for growth in length, not width -- it is the site of endochondral ossification that lengthens the shaft, a separate mechanism entirely from width growth.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The diaphysis is the shaft of the bone, the structure that grows, not the tissue layer that does the growing; naming it does not answer which structure drives appositional width growth.
explanations.D: Correct. The periosteum is the fibrous membrane covering the outer surface of a long bone, and its deep, osteogenic layer lays down new bone by appositional growth, which is what widens the shaft. This runs in parallel with, and independently of, length growth at the epiphyseal plate -- a fracture through the epiphyseal plate can stunt a bone's eventual length while its width continues to increase normally, because the periosteum is unaffected. Endosteal resorption on the inner surface enlarges the medullary cavity as the periosteum adds bone outside, keeping the cortical wall a roughly constant thickness as the whole bone widens.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The endosteum lines the internal (medullary) surface of the bone and is mainly resorptive during growth, hollowing out the marrow cavity as the shaft widens from the outside -- it is not the source of the new bone that increases the shaft's outer width.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the periosteum as the structure responsible for growth of a long bone in thickness.

questions.title: Identifying a synovial joint
questions.question: Which of the following is a synovial joint?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The intervertebral discs form a secondary cartilaginous joint (a symphysis), not a synovial joint -- they lack a joint cavity and are joined by fibrocartilage.
explanations.B: Correct. The intercarpal joints, between adjacent carpal bones, are synovial plane joints: freely mobile, with a joint cavity and capsule, and their bone ends covered by hyaline articular cartilage. This is exactly the structural definition that separates a synovial joint from the cartilaginous and fibrous joints listed alongside it in this question -- the presence of a true joint cavity, not simply the fact that two bones meet.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The middle radioulnar region is spanned by the interosseous membrane, a fibrous syndesmosis, not a synovial joint (the proximal and distal radioulnar joints, at the ends of the forearm, are synovial pivot joints, but the shaft-level connection is not).
explanations.D: Incorrect. The epiphyseal plate is a primary cartilaginous joint (a synchondrosis), made of hyaline cartilage, allowing bone growth rather than movement -- it has no joint cavity.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The inferior tibiofibular joint is a fibrous syndesmosis, held by an interosseous ligament rather than possessing a synovial cavity.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the intercarpal joints as an example of a synovial joint.

questions.title: Joint type that allows rotation
questions.question: Which of the following joints allow rotation?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Plane joints permit only small gliding movements between flat or near-flat surfaces (such as the intercarpal or acromioclavicular joints), not rotation around an axis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hinge joints (such as the elbow) are uniaxial, moving only in flexion-extension around a single transverse axis, not rotation.
explanations.C: Correct. The pivot joint is the synovial joint type built specifically for rotation: one bone's ring or process rotates around a longitudinal axis, held by an osteoligamentous ring formed by the other bone plus an encircling ligament. The proximal and distal radioulnar joints (giving pronation and supination) and the atlantoaxial joint (giving side-to-side head rotation) are the classic examples. Unlike a ball-and-socket joint, a pivot joint has only this one rotational axis and no independent flexion-extension or abduction-adduction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Condyloid joints (such as the metacarpophalangeal joints) allow two axes of movement, flexion-extension plus abduction-adduction, but not independent rotation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A synchondrosis is a primary cartilaginous joint (such as the epiphyseal plate), essentially immobile and built for growth, not movement of any kind, let alone rotation.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the pivot joint as the synovial joint type that permits rotation.

questions.title: The vessel that contains oxygenated blood
questions.question: Which of the following vessels contains oxygenated blood?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The pulmonary artery is the one artery in the body that carries deoxygenated blood, from the right ventricle to the lungs to be oxygenated -- the opposite pattern from every other artery.
explanations.B: Correct. The pulmonary veins are the sole exception among all the body's veins: rather than returning deoxygenated blood to the heart like every other vein, the four pulmonary veins carry newly oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. This exception exists because the pulmonary circulation runs in the opposite functional direction from the systemic circulation -- the lungs, not a body tissue, are what these vessels are draining.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The superior vena cava is a systemic vein, returning deoxygenated blood from the head, neck and upper limbs to the right atrium, following the normal rule for veins.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The inferior vena cava is likewise a systemic vein, returning deoxygenated blood from the lower body to the right atrium.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The dural venous sinuses drain deoxygenated venous blood from the brain into the internal jugular veins, following the same normal venous rule as any other systemic vein.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the pulmonary veins as the only vessels carrying oxygenated blood among named veins.

questions.title: Lymph drainage that bypasses the thoracic duct
questions.question: Lymph from which one of the following regions doesn't drain into the thoracic duct?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The left side of the head drains into the thoracic duct, which collects everything outside the right lymphatic duct's small territory.
explanations.B: Correct. The right lymphatic duct drains only one quadrant of the body -- the right side of the head and neck, the right half of the thorax, and the right upper limb -- emptying separately into the venous system near the right subclavian/internal jugular junction. The thoracic duct drains everything else: the left side of the head and neck, the left upper limb, the left half of the thorax, and the whole body below the diaphragm (both lower limbs, abdomen and pelvis). Because the right upper limb falls specifically within the right lymphatic duct's one-quadrant territory, its lymph does not pass through the thoracic duct at all.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The left upper limb is outside the right lymphatic duct's territory, so like the rest of the "other three quadrants," it drains into the thoracic duct.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The right lower limb is below the diaphragm, which is thoracic duct territory regardless of right/left side, so it drains into the thoracic duct.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The left lower limb, likewise below the diaphragm, drains into the thoracic duct.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the right upper limb as lymph territory drained by the right lymphatic duct, not the thoracic duct.

questions.title: The normal site of implantation
questions.question: Which one of the following is the normal site of implantation?

options.A: The endometrium of the lower segment of the uterus
options.B: The endometrium of the upper part of the uterine body
options.C: The ampulla of the fallopian tube
options.D: The ovarian stroma near its cortex
options.E: The peritoneal cavity near the pelvic viscera

explanations.A: Incorrect. Implantation in the lower uterine segment, near the internal cervical os, is an abnormal low-lying site that produces placenta previa, not the normal implantation site.
explanations.B: Correct. The blastocyst normally implants in the endometrium of the upper part of the body of the uterus, usually on the posterior wall -- the site richest in glandular, well-vascularised endometrium during the secretory phase of the cycle, which best supports early nutrition of the conceptus before the placenta is fully established. This is the reference site against which every abnormal implantation location (too low in the uterus, or entirely outside it) is defined.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Implantation in the ampulla of the uterine tube is a tubal (ampullary) ectopic pregnancy, the most common form of ectopic pregnancy, not the normal site -- fertilization occurs in the ampulla, but implantation should not.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Implantation on the ovary itself is a rare form of ectopic pregnancy (ovarian pregnancy), entirely outside the uterine cavity.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Implantation in the peritoneal cavity is abdominal ectopic pregnancy, the rarest and most dangerous form of ectopic pregnancy, again entirely outside the uterus.

questions.learning_objective: State the normal implantation site as the endometrium of the upper uterine body.

questions.title: Spermatogenic cell formed by the second meiotic division
questions.question: Which spermatogenic cell of the following is the result of the second meiotic division?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Spermatogonia type A are the diploid stem cells at the very start of the lineage, produced by mitotic division of the original spermatogonia, not by any meiotic division.
explanations.B: Correct. A secondary spermatocyte completes the SECOND meiotic division -- separating sister chromatids, with no further DNA replication beforehand -- to produce a spermatid, a genuinely haploid cell (23 single chromosomes). This is distinct from the first meiotic division, which is what created the secondary spermatocyte itself (from the primary spermatocyte) by halving the chromosome number to 23, still duplicated. It is specifically this second, equational division that turns a secondary spermatocyte into a spermatid.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Primary spermatocytes are the diploid cells (46 chromosomes, each duplicated) that undergo the FIRST meiotic division, not its result -- they are the starting cell of meiosis I, not its product.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Secondary spermatocytes are themselves the product of the first meiotic division, not the second; they are the cell that then goes on to complete the second division.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Spermatogonia type B are an intermediate mitotic stage that gives rise to primary spermatocytes, produced by mitosis rather than by either meiotic division.

questions.learning_objective: State that a secondary spermatocyte produces a spermatid by completing the second meiotic division.

questions.title: What is true of the zona reaction
questions.question: Which one of the following is true regarding the zona reaction?

options.B: It includes the release of zona lysine by sperm
options.C: By it the zona pellucida becomes more rigid
options.D: It occurs in the uterine cavity
options.E: It is followed by sperm penetration

explanations.A: Incorrect. The zona reaction occurs immediately after fertilization (specifically after the first sperm fuses with the oocyte membrane), not immediately after ovulation, which happens earlier and involves no sperm at all.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The zona reaction is triggered by cortical granule release from the oocyte itself, not by a lysine released by sperm -- the oocyte, not the sperm, is the active party in this specific reaction.
explanations.C: Correct. Once the first sperm fuses with the oocyte membrane, cortical granule release changes the chemical structure of the zona pellucida -- the zona reaction -- making it harder and more resistant to further sperm penetration. This is the mechanism that blocks polyspermy: the zona pellucida's altered, rigidified state prevents any additional sperm from binding or penetrating it. Before implantation, the intact, hardened zona also keeps the dividing blastomeres from adhering prematurely to the tubal mucosa.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The zona reaction takes place at the site of fertilization, in the ampulla of the uterine tube, not in the uterine cavity, which the conceptus has not yet reached at this stage.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The zona reaction is followed by the blocking of further sperm penetration, not by penetration -- it is precisely the mechanism that prevents any additional sperm from penetrating after the first has succeeded.

questions.learning_objective: State that the zona reaction makes the zona pellucida more rigid, blocking further sperm penetration.

questions.title: Event of the second week after fertilization
questions.question: Which one of the following occurs during the second week after fertilization?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Gastrulation, which forms the trilaminar germ disc, begins in the third week of development, not the second.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cleavage, the series of mitotic divisions of the zygote, occurs during the first week, ending with formation of the blastocyst before it reaches the uterine cavity -- it is complete before the second week begins.
explanations.C: Correct. The second week of development, sometimes called "the week of twos," is when the bilaminar germ disc forms together with the amniotic cavity (from the epiblast) and the primary yolk sac (from the hypoblast). This places amniotic cavity formation squarely in a fixed weekly sequence: after cleavage (week 1) and before gastrulation (week 3) and folding (week 4).
explanations.D: Incorrect. The notochord develops during gastrulation, which begins in the third week, not the second.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Folding of the flat trilaminar disc into a three-dimensional body occurs in the fourth week, well after the second week's amniotic cavity/bilaminar disc formation.

questions.learning_objective: Place amniotic cavity development in the second week after fertilization.

questions.title: Organelle responsible for modifying and packaging secretory proteins
questions.question: Which organelle is responsible for the modification and packaging of secretory proteins?

explanations.A: Correct. Once a protein destined for secretion is synthesised by ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum, it is transported to the Golgi apparatus, which further modifies it (glycosylation, sulfation and proteolytic processing among other steps), sorts it, and packages the finished product into membrane-bound secretory vesicles that bud from its trans face for release from the cell. The rough ER only synthesises and does initial folding; it is specifically the Golgi that carries out the modification and final packaging step the question asks about. This same rER-to-Golgi route is followed whether the final product is a general secretory protein or, as a special case, a lysosomal digestive enzyme.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lysosomes are themselves a packaged product of this pathway (containing digestive enzymes made by rER and packaged by the Golgi); they store enzymes for digestion rather than modifying and packaging proteins for secretion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Peroxisomes carry out oxidative detoxification reactions (breaking down hydrogen peroxide and long-chain fatty acids), a function unrelated to modifying and packaging secretory proteins.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The plasma membrane is the site where secretory vesicles ultimately fuse to release their contents by exocytosis, but it does not itself modify or package the protein beforehand.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum specialises in lipid synthesis and drug detoxification (via cytochrome P450 enzymes), not in modifying or packaging proteins, which is instead the job of the rough ER (synthesis) and Golgi (modification/packaging).

questions.learning_objective: Identify the Golgi apparatus as the organelle that modifies and packages secretory proteins.

questions.title: What is true of the cell membrane
questions.question: Which of the following is true about the cell membrane?

options.A: Surrounds the nucleus in a single layer
options.B: Surrounds the individual ribosomes within the cell
options.C: Structurally based on a lipid bilayer
options.D: Structurally based on a protein only

explanations.A: Incorrect. The structure surrounding the nucleus is the nuclear envelope, a double membrane with nuclear pores, not the cell (plasma) membrane, and it is not what the cell membrane itself does.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ribosomes are not individually surrounded by membrane at all -- they are membrane-free ribonucleoprotein particles, free in the cytosol or attached to the outer face of the rough endoplasmic reticulum, never enclosed by the cell membrane.
explanations.C: Correct. The cell membrane is structurally a phospholipid bilayer, with hydrophilic heads facing the aqueous solution on either side and hydrophobic tails directed inward, plus cholesterol interspersed among the fatty acid tails to buffer fluidity, and peripheral and integral proteins providing structural and channel/carrier functions. This lipid bilayer is the defining structural feature of the membrane -- protein and carbohydrate are important components, but the bilayer itself is built of lipid.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The membrane is not protein alone -- protein makes up roughly half its mass, but the structural framework is the phospholipid bilayer, with protein embedded in or attached to it, not a protein-only structure.
explanations.E: Incorrect (the source prints this option's letter as "a," a duplicate of option A's letter -- read here as the fifth option by position). The glycocalyx is the membrane's carbohydrate coat, not its protein component; it is built of oligosaccharide chains attached to membrane lipids and proteins, sitting on the external surface, distinct from the membrane's protein constituents themselves.

questions.learning_objective: State that the cell membrane is structurally based on a phospholipid bilayer.

questions.title: Cause of localized cytoplasmic basophilia
questions.question: The presence of which of the following causes localized cytoplasmic basophilia?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Mitochondria are acidophilic (eosinophilic) on routine staining, owing to their protein-rich cristae, not basophilic, so their presence does not produce basophilia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The Golgi apparatus is essentially invisible on routine H&E staining (it requires silver impregnation to be seen at all) and is not itself a source of basophilic staining.
explanations.C: Correct. Rough endoplasmic reticulum carries ribosomes attached to its surface, and ribosomes are what make cytoplasm basophilic, because of the acidity of the phosphate groups in their ribosomal RNA. Because rough ER occupies a defined region of the cytoplasm rather than being spread evenly throughout it, a concentration of attached ribosomes on rER produces localized (focal) basophilia in that region, in contrast to the diffuse basophilia produced by free ribosomes scattered through the cytosol.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum has no attached ribosomes by definition (that is what makes it "smooth"), so it does not contribute to cytoplasmic basophilia at all.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Lysosomes are membrane-bound digestive vesicles without a concentration of ribosomal RNA, so their presence is not a cause of basophilic staining.

questions.learning_objective: Identify rough endoplasmic reticulum as the cause of localized cytoplasmic basophilia.

questions.title: Structure formed by digestion of fluid material
questions.question: Which of the following is formed as a result of the digestion of fluid material?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A primary lysosome is the starting enzyme-containing vesicle, formed by the rER-Golgi pathway before any digestion has taken place, not a product of digesting fluid material.
explanations.B: Correct. A secondary lysosome is classified by what its primary lysosome fused with: a multivesicular body is specifically a primary lysosome fused with a pinocytic vesicle, digesting fluid material that the cell took up by pinocytosis. This is distinct from a heterolysosome (fused with a phagosome, digesting solid particles) and an autolysosome (fused with the cell's own old organelles) -- the multivesicular body is the one named specifically for fluid-phase digestion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An autophagic vacuole (autolysosome) forms from a primary lysosome fusing with the cell's own worn-out organelles, digesting the cell's own solid structural material, not extracellular fluid.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A phagosome is the vesicle formed by phagocytosis of a solid particle, before it has even fused with a lysosome -- it is the input to digestion of a solid particle, not a product of fluid digestion.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A heterophagic vacuole (heterolysosome) forms from a primary lysosome fusing with a phagosome, digesting solid extracellular material taken in by phagocytosis, not fluid material.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the multivesicular body as the secondary lysosome formed by digestion of fluid material.

questions.title: What is true of ribosomes
questions.question: Which of the following is true concerning ribosomes?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ribosomes are basophilic, not acidophilic -- their ribosomal RNA carries acidic phosphate groups that bind basic dyes, which is what basophilic staining means (an easy point to reason backwards on if "acid" is read as meaning "acidophilic").
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ribosomes are not membrane-bound organelles at all; they are ribonucleoprotein particles free of any surrounding membrane, whether they lie free in the cytosol or are attached to the outer, cytosolic face of the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
explanations.C: Incorrect. As with option B, ribosomes have no surrounding membrane, single or double -- membrane-bound organelles are things like mitochondria (double membrane) or lysosomes (single membrane), a different category from ribosomes entirely.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ribosomes attach to the rough endoplasmic reticulum, not to the Golgi apparatus; the Golgi apparatus receives finished proteins from rER by vesicular transport rather than carrying ribosomes on its own surface.
explanations.E: Correct. Ribosomes are basophilic organelles: their ribosomal RNA carries acidic phosphate groups that bind basic dyes strongly, producing basophilic staining wherever ribosomes concentrate. Free ribosomes scattered through the cytosol produce a diffuse basophilia, while ribosomes attached to rough ER produce a more localized, focal basophilia -- but in both cases it is the ribosome's RNA that is responsible.

questions.learning_objective: State that ribosomes are basophilic organelles, owing to their RNA content.

questions.title: What is true of chromatin
questions.question: Which of the following is true concerning chromatin?

options.D: It is attached to the outer nuclear membrane

explanations.A: Incorrect. Chromatin is basophilic, not acidophilic, because of the phosphate groups of its nucleic acid (DNA), which bind basic dyes -- the opposite staining affinity from what this option claims.
explanations.B: Correct. Euchromatin is the extended, uncoiled form of chromatin, carrying the genes that are actively being transcribed; it predominates in metabolically active, protein-forming cells, appears as fine pale-staining threads giving a vesicular nucleus with a clear nucleolus, and is electron-lucent. This active/extended state is the defining feature that distinguishes euchromatin from its coiled, inactive counterpart, heterochromatin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Heterochromatin is the coiled, condensed, INACTIVE form of chromatin -- the reverse of this option's claim -- predominating in metabolically quiet cells such as the small lymphocyte, and giving a condensed nucleus with dark clumps and an unclear nucleolus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Peripheral heterochromatin is attached to the INNER surface of the nuclear membrane (one of the three named sites of heterochromatin), not the outer surface, and this is true of only the heterochromatin subtype, not chromatin as a whole.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Chromatin is a nucleoprotein -- double-stranded DNA complexed with histone and non-histone protein -- not a lipid; lipid is not a structural component of chromatin at all.

questions.learning_objective: State that euchromatin is the extended, transcriptionally active form of chromatin.

questions.title: Role of microtubules
questions.question: Microtubules have an important role in which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Carbohydrate metabolism (glycolysis, glycogen handling) takes place in the cytosol using soluble enzymes, not the cytoskeletal microtubule system.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Oxidative phosphorylation occurs on the inner mitochondrial membrane's electron transport chain, a function of mitochondria, not of microtubules.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Water balance across the cell membrane depends on osmotic gradients and membrane channels (such as aquaporins), not on the microtubule cytoskeleton.
explanations.D: Correct. Centrioles, each a cylinder of nine microtubule triplets (27 microtubules in total), duplicate during S phase and organise the microtubules of the mitotic spindle -- the apparatus that pulls duplicated chromosomes apart to the two daughter cells during division. This is a direct, mechanical role that intermediate filaments (keratin, vimentin, glial fibrillary acidic protein, desmin) do not share, which is exactly why loss of microtubule/spindle function halts mitosis outright and is exploited by microtubule-targeting anti-cancer drugs.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Drug detoxification of lipid-soluble substances is carried out by cytochrome P450 enzymes on the smooth endoplasmic reticulum, not by microtubules.

questions.learning_objective: Identify mitotic spindle formation as a key role of microtubules, via the centriole.

questions.title: Stain used to demonstrate glycogen
questions.question: Glycogen can be demonstrated by which one of the following stains?

explanations.A: Correct. Best's carmine is a histochemical stain specific to glycogen, staining glycogen granules in a tissue section a distinct red colour. It is one of several named stains each used for a different target substance, and among the options listed here it is the one specifically associated with glycogen.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Osmic acid demonstrates lipid (fat), not glycogen or any other carbohydrate -- it is one of the classic fat stains, not a carbohydrate stain.
explanations.C: Incorrect. H&E (haematoxylin and eosin) is the general-purpose structural stain used for routine histology, not a substance-specific stain for any one target such as glycogen.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sudan III, like osmic acid, is a lipid stain, demonstrating neutral fat rather than glycogen.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Silver stains are used to demonstrate reticular fibres in connective tissue, or, in the nervous system, neurofibrils -- not glycogen.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Best's carmine as the stain used to demonstrate glycogen.

questions.title: Result of abnormal transverse division of the centromere
questions.question: Abnormal transverse division of the centromere results in the formation of which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Translocation results from an exchange of material between two non-homologous chromosomes, a mechanism unrelated to how the centromere itself divides.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Deletion results from the loss of a chromosome segment, again a different mechanism from an abnormal plane of centromere division.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A ring chromosome forms when the two broken ends of a single chromosome fuse together into a circle, not from an abnormal centromere division plane.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Inversion results from a chromosome segment breaking out and reinserting in reversed orientation, a distinct mechanism from centromere division.
explanations.E: Correct. A centromere normally divides longitudinally (along the chromosome's long axis), separating the two sister chromatids so each daughter cell receives one copy of each chromosome arm. An isochromosome results when the centromere instead divides transversely (across its short axis), producing one chromosome with two copies of one arm and none of the other, plus a reciprocal chromosome with two copies of the other arm. This distinguishes an isochromosome mechanically from translocation, deletion, ring-chromosome formation and inversion, each of which arises from a different structural error.

questions.learning_objective: State that transverse (rather than longitudinal) centromere division produces an isochromosome.

questions.title: What the Barr body is
questions.question: What is the Barr body?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The Barr body is the INACTIVE X chromosome, not the active one -- exactly one X stays active in every cell, and it is the other, switched-off X that condenses and is seen as the Barr body.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The Barr body is specifically an X chromosome, never a Y chromosome; the Y chromosome is not inactivated in this way.
explanations.C: Correct. The Barr body (sex chromatin) is an X chromosome that has been inactivated and condensed into a mass of heterochromatin, seen as a dark plaque against the inner nuclear membrane in most cells (and as a drumstick appendage on the nucleus in a proportion of female neutrophils). Because exactly one X stays active in every cell, the Barr body count always equals the number of X chromosomes minus one: a normal male (XY) has none, a normal female (XX) has one, and a Klinefelter male (XXY) has one as well, since he carries an extra, inactivated X.
explanations.D: Incorrect. As with option B, the Y chromosome is not the structure involved -- the Barr body is always derived from an X chromosome, and "active Y" describes neither its identity nor its inactivation status.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The Barr body is a sex chromosome (specifically X), not an autosome; autosomes are not inactivated in this X-inactivation process.

questions.learning_objective: Define the Barr body as an inactivated X chromosome.

questions.title: What the mother cell gives rise to in meiosis
questions.question: In meiosis, the mother cell gives rise to which of the following?

options.A: 2 daughter cells with the haploid number of chromosomes
options.B: 4 daughter cells with the diploid number of chromosomes
options.C: 4 daughter cells with the haploid number of chromosomes
options.D: 2 daughter cells with the diploid number of chromosomes
options.E: 3 daughter cells with the haploid number of chromosomes

explanations.A: Incorrect. Meiosis produces four daughter cells, not two -- two daughter cells is the result of a single mitotic division, not the two sequential divisions of meiosis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The daughter cells of meiosis are haploid, not diploid; producing diploid daughter cells is what mitosis does, not meiosis, which is specifically the reduction division.
explanations.C: Correct. Meiosis is a two-division process (meiosis I, reductional, then meiosis II, equational) by which one diploid germ-line mother cell produces four genetically distinct daughter cells, each with the haploid chromosome number. In spermatogenesis all four mature into functional sperm; in oogenesis the same four-cell outcome occurs cytologically, but unequal cytoplasmic division means only one becomes a functional mature ovum, with the other three becoming non-functional polar bodies.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This combines two errors at once: meiosis produces four cells, not two, and those cells are haploid, not diploid -- two diploid daughter cells is instead the result of ordinary mitosis.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Meiosis produces four daughter cells cytologically, not three, even though in oogenesis only one of the four becomes a functional ovum (the other three are polar bodies, not simply absent).

questions.learning_objective: State that meiosis produces four haploid daughter cells from one diploid mother cell.

questions.title: Cells that cannot divide
questions.question: Which of the following cells cannot divide?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pancreatic cells are classed as stable (quiescent) cells: they do not divide continuously under normal conditions, but they retain the capacity to re-enter the cell cycle and proliferate when needed, unlike a truly permanent cell.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Liver cells are the classic example of a stable/quiescent cell population -- normally non-dividing, but capable of substantial regeneration and division after injury (such as partial hepatectomy), which is the opposite of "cannot divide."
explanations.C: Incorrect. Endocrine gland cells, like liver cells, are stable cells that can re-enter the cell cycle and divide when stimulated, not permanently non-dividing cells.
explanations.D: Correct. Cells are classified by renewal capacity into labile (continuously dividing), stable/quiescent (normally non-dividing but able to re-enter the cycle), and permanent cells, which have permanently exited the cell cycle after full differentiation. Mature nerve cells are the classic permanent cell: once fully differentiated, they cannot divide again, which is why neuronal loss (for example after a stroke or spinal cord injury) is not repaired by division of the remaining neurons.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Most epithelial cells are labile cells, among the most actively and continuously dividing cell populations in the body (for example the epidermis and gut lining), the opposite of cells that cannot divide.

questions.learning_objective: Identify nerve cells as permanent cells that cannot divide.
